title: Geopolitical energy disruption converts global interdependence into uneven household, business, and inflation exposure
source_unit: OECD Economic Outlook, Interim Report March 2026: Testing Resilience
geography: Global and G20 economies, with country comparisons across advanced and emerging economies and specific household-energy exposure analysis

observations.period: March 2026; Middle East conflict and energy-market disruption

denominator.unit: OECD interim outlook scenario and global economic assessment

energy_shock.value: The report says oil prices rose by over 50% between the conflict's onset and March 20, while gas prices rose sharply in Europe and Asia

supply_interdependence.value: Disruption affects energy, fertilisers, air transport, and other global supply chains because the Middle East is a major production and logistics hub

inflation_channel.value: Sustained disruption is expected to add to business costs and consumer-price inflation while weighing on growth

interpretation.value: Geopolitical risk is experienced domestically through infrastructure and commodity dependence, not only through military or diplomatic channels

observations.method: OECD combines national accounts, commodity and financial-market data, trade statistics, price databases, and a scenario-based macroeconomic projection using information available through March 23, 2026.
observations.uncertainty: The outlook is conditional on a technical energy-price path and uncertain conflict duration and breadth. It is a forecast and scenario assessment, not a realized causal decomposition of household welfare.
observations.subgroup: Effects differ by country, income, energy intensity, sector, import dependence, and exposure to transport, petrochemical, metals, and fertiliser markets.
observations.counterinterpretation: Strategic reserves, substitution, fiscal support, lower energy intensity, and a short-lived disruption could reduce the projected effects; price changes do not map one-for-one onto household living standards.

observations.period: 2026 projections; global growth and G20 inflation

global_growth.value: Global GDP growth is projected at 2.9% in 2026 and 3.0% in 2027

g20_inflation_revision.value: G20 headline inflation was revised upward by 1.2 percentage points for 2026 and 0.2 points for 2027 relative to the December 2025 outlook

technology_offset.value: Technology-related investment and production provide a growth impulse that partly offsets higher energy and fertiliser costs

interpretation.value: Resilience is uneven: aggregate growth can remain positive while household purchasing power and sectoral conditions deteriorate

observations.method: The OECD compares the March 2026 interim baseline with its December 2025 outlook using revised data and a technical assumption about oil and gas futures prices.
observations.uncertainty: Forecast revisions are sensitive to energy prices, conflict duration, policy responses, technology investment, and trade conditions. GDP growth is not a direct measure of distributional welfare or cultural confidence.
observations.subgroup: National and sectoral outcomes vary widely; the G20 aggregate obscures differences among energy importers, exporters, lower-income households, and energy-intensive firms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Positive growth and productivity gains in AI-adopting sectors could support wages or public revenues over time, even if near-term price pressure is regressive.

observations.period: Latest available household energy-basket comparisons in the OECD report

country_range.value: The share of energy in household consumption baskets ranges from around 12% in Brazil to 6% in Canada

distributional_exposure.value: Households at the lower end of the income distribution have a higher energy consumption share than those at the higher end

sector_exposure.value: Transport, petrochemicals, and metals manufacturing are identified as particularly exposed business sectors

interpretation.value: The same geopolitical shock creates different political and consumer pressures depending on household budget structure and national energy dependence

observations.method: The OECD uses consumer-price weights and country energy-mix information to compare energy shares in household consumption baskets and discusses income distribution and sectoral exposure.
observations.uncertainty: The energy-basket share is not the same as total exposure to an energy shock: fuel mix, pass-through, housing type, transport needs, subsidies, and substitution all matter. Country figures are not a uniform cross-national survey measure.
observations.subgroup: Lower-income households, energy-intensive households, renters or commuters, and residents of import-dependent economies may face different exposure than national averages suggest.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher energy shares can also reflect different accounting conventions, climate, transport systems, or household production patterns; the share alone does not establish hardship or political response.

observations.period: 2025–2026; AI adoption, productivity, labour demand, and policy response

denominator.unit: OECD report synthesis of labour, productivity, AI adoption, and policy evidence

ai_productivity.value: U.S. labour productivity growth has recently been faster in sectors with high AI adoption

labour_demand.value: Job-vacancy measures have eased in Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States, while unemployment remains low by historical standards

policy_buffer.value: Governments have announced emergency measures to cushion energy costs, adding pressure to public finances

interpretation.value: The transition combines productivity upside, labour-market uncertainty, and fiscal choices over who absorbs infrastructure and energy shocks

observations.method: The report combines sectoral productivity data, vacancy and unemployment indicators, policy announcements, and macroeconomic projections; the U.S. AI comparison uses BEA, BLS, and OECD calculations.
observations.uncertainty: The sectoral AI association is not a causal estimate of AI's productivity effect, and vacancy changes do not establish layoffs, job quality, or worker bargaining power. Policy measures may change as conditions evolve.
observations.subgroup: Impacts differ by occupation, sector, skill, geography, energy intensity, and access to social protection or employer support.
observations.counterinterpretation: Productivity gains could support employment and wages over time; easing vacancies may reflect normalization rather than deterioration, and fiscal support can prevent deeper household losses.

boundary: This record adds an official macro-to-household pathway linking geopolitical conflict, energy and fertiliser dependence, inflation, growth, sectoral exposure, AI productivity, labour demand, and fiscal buffering. It does not provide respondent-level data, a causal household-welfare estimate, a political-opinion measure, or a forecast that remains valid if conflict and energy conditions change.
